system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2184-03-12 18:17:00 to 2184-03-13 14:19:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with fevers and hypotension during dialysis, found to have MRSA bacteremia likely originating from his right femoral dialysis catheter. He was treated with vancomycin and initially retained the line despite purulence, but developed hypotension requiring MICU care. The infected catheter was removed, followed by a temporary line and two line holidays due to persistent positive cultures. Surveillance cultures eventually cleared, and a new tunneled left femoral dialysis catheter was placed. Echocardiograms showed no evidence of endocarditis, and heart function remained stable. The patient completed antibiotic therapy with vancomycin dosed through dialysis, and was discharged to an extended care facility on a four-week course with weekly monitoring of CBC and vancomycin levels. He restarted lisinopril and continued management of comorbidities including ESRD, systolic heart failure, and seizure disorder.
problems: Infection and inflammatory reaction due to other vascular device, implant, and graft
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy

mediastinum is unremarkable.  The cardiac silhouette is within normal limits
for size.  There is distal tip of apparent femoral-approach catheter
projecting along the right heart, stable from prior exams.  Please note, while
this is present on multiple more remote exams, this line was not present on
the ___ study.  It is otherwise grossly stable.  No effusion or
pneumothorax is seen.

IMPRESSION:  Limited study due to low lung volumes.  Bibasilar atelectasis is
seen.  There is no discrete focal consolidation.  There may be mild edema
versus central vascular congestion.  Central line as above.

INDICATION:  ___ male with two seizures today.  Evaluate for
intracranial hemorrhage.

COMPARISON:  ___.

NON-CONTRAST HEAD CT:

There is no intracranial hemorrhage, parenchymal edema, or mass effect.  There
is diffuse prominence of the sulci and ventricles, stable from ___, and
compatible with global atrophy.  Periventricular white matter hypodensities
are also noted, likely reflecting the sequelae of chronic small vessel
infarcts.  There is no shift of midline structures, and the basal cisterns
remain patent.  There are no abnormal extra-axial fluid collections.  The
visualized paranasal sinuses and mastoids are notable for partial
opacification of the right anterior ethmoid air cells and left sphenoid sinus,
as on prior study.  They are otherwise well aerated.  There are no calvarial
or skull base fractures identified.  Note is made of extensive pneumatization
of the petrous temporal bones.

IMPRESSION:  No acute intracranial process, including no hemorrhage. 
Extensive atrophy and mild sinus disease are stable from prior studies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. You were brought in after having a seizure during dialysis. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I was almost done with dialysis and then everything went blank. I heard I had a seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you did. The staff at your rehab facility said you didn’t get your seizure medication this morning. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… yeah. They gave me the wrong dose. I’ve been okay for months. Last seizure was about six months ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely why this happened. We’ve restarted your regular meds—Keppra and Trileptal. You’re on a monitor now to make sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay now. No headache or weakness. But I’m worried—could this happen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The risk is lower as long as you get your medications on time. We’ll make sure your rehab team knows how important that is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a head CT to check for bleeding or stroke. Good news—it’s normal. No hemorrhage or swelling in the brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my heart? I remember someone saying something about an EKG change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right after the seizure, your heart rate spiked and there were some changes on the EKG—ST depressions in leads V4–V6.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a heart attack? I’ve had one before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your troponin was slightly elevated at 0.12, but cardiology reviewed it and thinks it’s due to the high heart rate during the seizure, not a new heart attack. The EKG changes resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart? Just the seizure affecting it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stress on the heart from seizures can cause temporary changes. We started a heparin bridge just to be safe, and you got aspirin too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a quiet night—no more seizures. Your labs are stable, and you’re alert and doing well. We’re planning to send you back to the rehab facility today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No changes to my meds? I want to make sure this doesn’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your seizure meds the same—Levetiracetam and Oxcarbazepine—and adding an extra dose after dialysis, which helps maintain levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And I should keep weighing myself every morning, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Call your doctor if you gain more than three pounds in a day. We also want you to stay on all your other medications for heart, kidneys, and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure the nurses at rehab know to give me my meds on time. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. We’re discharging you back to the same facility. You’re alert, walking with your walker, and in good shape otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge papers are ready. No new diagnoses, and we didn’t need any procedures. It was mainly about stabilizing you after the seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll be more careful and make sure my meds are right from now on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything feels off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—was my brain scan really okay? I’ve had strokes before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the CT showed no bleeding or new stroke. There’s some expected brain atrophy and old changes from small vessel disease, but nothing new or urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. But you’re stable, and we’re confident sending you back with your full medication plan.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted after experiencing a seizure during hemodialysis, which was likely due to missing his morning dose of antiepileptic medication at his rehab facility. He was treated with IM Ativan in the ER and resumed his home seizure medications. Post-ictal EKG showed transient ST depressions and a mildly elevated troponin, but cardiology attributed these to tachycardia during the seizure rather than acute ischemia. A non-contrast head CT ruled out intracranial hemorrhage or acute stroke, showing only stable chronic changes. The patient remained seizure-free during admission, with no cardiac complications. His medication regimen was continued without changes, with reinforcement of post-dialysis dosing. He was discharged back to his extended care facility with instructions to monitor weight and ensure medication adherence.
